Robust and stochastic optimization

Source: vignettes/robust-stochastic.Rmd
robust-stochastic.Rmd
library(optcompR)

Uncertain data can be handled in two ways. Robust optimization asks a constraint to hold for every value in an uncertainty set. Stochastic optimization treats the data as random and constrains or optimizes probabilities, expectations or risk measures. optcompR provides the standard exact reformulations of both, built from ordinary variables, rows and cones, so any capable solver handles the result. Each function says whether its reformulation is exact or an approximation.

Function Model Reformulation Exact?
opt_robust_constraint(..., "box") a \in [a_0 - \delta, a_0 + \delta] linear yes
opt_robust_constraint(..., "budget") at most \Gamma deviations linear (duality) yes
opt_robust_constraint(..., "ellipsoid") a = a_0 + Pu,\ \|u\| \le 1 second-order cone yes
opt_chance_constraint(..., "gaussian") a \sim N(\mu, \Sigma) second-order cone yes, for p \ge 0.5
opt_chance_constraint(..., "scenario") sampled a one row per sample approximation
opt_cvar() conditional value at risk linear (Rockafellar and Uryasev) yes
opt_expectation() sample average linear yes for the sample
opt_worst_expectation() finite ambiguity set epigraph yes

Robust linear constraints

A production plan uses two resources whose consumption per unit is uncertain: nominally one unit each, but up to 0.5 and 0.2 more. With a box uncertainty set the constraint must hold for the worst coefficients, which for nonnegative production are the largest ones:

m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, lower = 0)
opt_robust_constraint(m, x, a0 = c(1, 1), b = 10, delta = c(0.5, 0.2))
opt_objective(m, 3 * x[1] + 2.8 * x[2])
r <- opt_solve(m)
opt_value(r, x)
#> [1] 0.000000 8.333333
opt_objective_value(r)
#> [1] 23.33333

The reformulation is a_0^\top x + \delta^\top s \le b with s \ge |x|, so it is valid for variables of either sign.

Budgeted uncertainty

Protecting against every coefficient at its worst at once is often too conservative. The budget set of Bertsimas and Sim allows at most \Gamma coefficients to deviate. \Gamma = 0 is the nominal problem and \Gamma = n the box:

budget <- function(gamma) {
  m <- opt_model("max")
  x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 3, lower = 0)
  opt_robust_constraint(m, x, a0 = c(1, 1, 1), b = 6, delta = c(1, 1, 1),
                        uncertainty = "budget", gamma = gamma)
  opt_objective(m, sum(x))
  opt_objective_value(opt_solve(m))
}
sapply(c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3), budget)
#> [1] 6.000000 5.142857 4.500000 3.600000 3.000000

Ellipsoidal uncertainty

With a = a_0 + Pu and \|u\|_2 \le 1, the worst case of a^\top x is a_0^\top x + \|P^\top x\|_2, a second-order cone:

m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, lower = 0)
P <- diag(c(0.5, 0.2))
opt_robust_constraint(m, x, a0 = c(1, 1), b = 10, uncertainty = "ellipsoid",
                      P = P)
opt_objective(m, 3 * x[1] + 2.8 * x[2])
r <- opt_solve(m)
v <- opt_value(r, x)
v
#> [1] 1.617836 6.799810
sum(v) + sqrt(sum((t(P) %*% v)^2))  # the worst case is exactly 10
#> [1] 10
opt_objective_value(r)
#> [1] 23.89298

The ellipsoid is smaller than the box with the same half-widths, so the robust plan is less conservative.

Chance constraints

A chance constraint asks P(a^\top x \le b) \ge p. For Gaussian coefficients a \sim N(\mu, \Sigma) it is equivalent to \mu^\top x + \Phi^{-1}(p) \|\Sigma^{1/2} x\|_2 \le b, a convex second-order cone when p \ge 0.5:

Sigma <- matrix(c(0.04, 0.01, 0.01, 0.02), 2)
m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, lower = 0)
opt_chance_constraint(m, x, b = 10, prob = 0.95, mean = c(1, 1),
                      Sigma = Sigma)
opt_objective(m, sum(x))
v <- opt_value(opt_solve(m), x)
v
#> [1] 2.053234 6.159687
pnorm((10 - sum(v)) / sqrt(drop(t(v) %*% Sigma %*% v)))
#> [1] 0.95

The achieved probability is exactly the requested 0.95. A Monte Carlo check agrees:

set.seed(1)
a <- matrix(rnorm(2e5), ncol = 2) %*% chol(Sigma) + 1
mean(a %*% v <= 10)
#> [1] 0.94994

For other distributions the scenario approach imposes the constraint for each of N samples. It is an approximation: with d decision variables the solution satisfies the chance constraint at level 1 - \epsilon with confidence 1 - \beta when N \ge \frac{2}{\epsilon}(\ln\frac1\beta + d) (Calafiore and Campi). The bound is the user’s to check; optcompR does not claim it.

set.seed(2)
S <- matrix(rexp(2 * 300), ncol = 2)  # skewed coefficients
m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, lower = 0)
opt_chance_constraint(m, x, b = 10, samples = S, method = "scenario")
opt_objective(m, sum(x))
v <- opt_value(opt_solve(m), x)
v
#> [1] 1.154559 1.542164
# out of sample probability of violation
mean(matrix(rexp(2e5), ncol = 2) %*% v > 10)
#> [1] 0.00558

Risk measures over scenarios

Sample average approximation

Given K loss scenarios L_k(x), opt_expectation() is their (weighted) average; minimizing it is sample average approximation.

Conditional value at risk

The conditional value at risk at level \alpha is the expected loss in the worst 1 - \alpha fraction of outcomes. Rockafellar and Uryasev showed

\mathrm{CVaR}_\alpha(L) = \min_t\ t + \frac{1}{1-\alpha} \sum_k p_k (L_k - t)_+ ,

which opt_cvar() writes with an auxiliary variable for t and one per scenario for the excess. Minimizing it, or bounding it from above, is exact. A portfolio over four return scenarios:

R <- matrix(c(0.10, 0.02, -0.05, 0.04,
              0.03, 0.01,  0.02, 0.01), 4,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("stock", "bond")))
cvar_portfolio <- function(alpha) {
  m <- opt_model()
  w <- opt_variable(m, "w", dim = 2, lower = 0)
  opt_constraint(m, sum(w) == 1)
  loss <- -(R %*% w)
  opt_objective(m, opt_cvar(m, loss, alpha = alpha))
  r <- opt_solve(m)
  c(opt_value(r, w), cvar = opt_objective_value(r))
}
rbind(`alpha = 0.25` = cvar_portfolio(0.25),
      `alpha = 0.75` = cvar_portfolio(0.75))
#>                                 cvar
#> alpha = 0.25 0.000 1.000 -0.01333333
#> alpha = 0.75 0.125 0.875 -0.01125000

At \alpha = 0.75 only the worst scenario counts and the portfolio moves toward bonds. CVaR can also be a constraint: maximize expected return subject to a CVaR limit.

m <- opt_model("max")
w <- opt_variable(m, "w", dim = 2, lower = 0)
opt_constraint(m, sum(w) == 1)
opt_constraint(m, opt_cvar(m, -(R %*% w), alpha = 0.75) <= 0.01)
opt_objective(m, opt_expectation(R %*% w))
opt_value(opt_solve(m), w)
#> [1] 0.4285714 0.5714286

A CVaR expression must appear where a larger value is worse (minimized, or on the left of <=). Maximizing it is not modeled by this formulation, because the auxiliary variables can then inflate it.

Distributionally robust expectations

When the scenario probabilities are themselves uncertain, opt_worst_expectation() takes a matrix of candidate distributions and returns the largest expected loss among them, which is also the worst case over their convex hull:

probs <- rbind(uniform = rep(0.25, 4),
               crash   = c(0.1, 0.1, 0.7, 0.1),
               boom    = c(0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
m <- opt_model()
w <- opt_variable(m, "w", dim = 2, lower = 0)
opt_constraint(m, sum(w) == 1)
opt_objective(m, opt_worst_expectation(m, -(R %*% w), probs))
r <- opt_solve(m)
opt_value(r, w)
#> [1] 0.03125 0.96875
probs %*% (-(R %*% opt_value(r, w)))
#>               [,1]
#> uniform -0.0178125
#> crash   -0.0178125
#> boom    -0.0264375

The optimal weights equalize the expected loss under the two binding distributions.
